title: Supplementary material to "European runoff drought event types: From historical classification to projected future changes"
problem: Global Climate Models (GCMs) exhibit systematic biases in simulating European drought characteristics like duration, frequency, and severity compared to observations, revealing deficiencies that challenge the reliability of historical and future drought assessments.
method: This study classifies European runoff droughts into a process-based typology using hydrological model simulations, driven by observational and climate model data, to analyze historical characteristics and project future changes for different drought types under the RCP 4.5 scenario.
task: The task is to classify European runoff droughts into a typology, analyze their historical characteristics, and project how these drought types will change in the future under the RCP 4.5 climate scenario.

Supplement of: European runoff drought typology: historical classification and projected changes under RCP 4.5
Looking at the spatial patterns of drought duration for the historical period (1971–2000), Figure S4a reveal substantial variability across Europe.
Based on the EOBS gridded observational dataset, rainfall deficit droughts occur most frequently in the Mediterranean basin, with local totals often exceeding 11 events over the 30-year period.
Central Europe exhibits intermediate event counts, typically between 5 and 9.

A comparison between historical GCM simulations (GCM_hist) and EOBS observations reveals systematic biases in the simulated number of events. Most notably, GCMs markedly underestimate rainfall deficit droughts across the Mediterranean and Western-Central Europe, with local differences reaching as much as -9 to -13 events.
However, models show some amplification of duration patterns, particularly for rainfall deficit droughts in southern Europe and rain-to-snow droughts in northern regions.
